body.text: Survivors of the Darkness, the book says, “is not written out of literary ambition or to entertain a reader. It is written as a document of the Israeli genocide against the Palestinians”. Written by Wesam Afifa and translated by Husam Almadhoun, and published by LeftWord Books, Survivors of the Darkness is about the experience of Osama al-Sayed, a Palestinian journalist who was held in Israeli prisons, including Sde Teiman, from March 2024 to October 2025.

Osama was arrested on March 18, 2024, when Israeli forces launched an offensive on Gaza’s Al-Shifa Hospital complex. Entering the Sde Teiman detention camp, Osama was greeted with the words “Welcome to Hell.” What follows is the story of Osama and of Palestinians like him who, according to the book, were arrested on undisclosed charges and subjected to torture and humiliation until dignity is forgotten.

In Survivors of the Darkness, Osama gives a first-person account of the degrees and variations of torture in Israeli prisons. He spent about 19 months in various prisons, including Ofer and Ketziot, before his release on October 13, 2025, as part of the ceasefire deal. Osama says he was threatened with death if he spoke about what happened in prison. But Osama still found his voice to tell his story.

Osama is nearly 40 and holds a bachelor’s degree in journalism and media. He has spent 16 years in local and international television. Before his arrest, he directed nine current affairs and variety programmes and news bulletins, working on live and recorded broadcasts. He now directs short films for a production company. Osama’s latest project was a series of 30 films, The Sole Survivor.

Afifa has led Al-Aqsa Media Network for seven years and previously served as editor-in-chief of Al-Resalah newspaper for 12 years. His work focusses on Palestinian affairs and political analysis, and on documenting human experiences of war and imprisonment.
Excerpts from two email interviews with Osama and Afifa, respectively:
Osama al-Sayed
A year after your release, can you sleep? Are there simple things in daily life that you still struggle with?

A year after my release, I can only fall asleep when I see the first light of dawn. One night, sleep got the better of me. I woke from a nightmare in which I was back in prison, being tortured again. I regretted falling asleep that night. Afterwards, I promised myself I would stay awake until morning.

I’m still displaced. Every day in Gaza, we struggle to find water, get food, and charge a phone. Even a lighter to start a fire is hard to find. When you can find one, it costs $50. We still escape death several times a day.

As a television director trained to observe closely, did your eye for detail make the abuse in Israeli prisons more painful? Did it affect how you understood the way your surroundings were used against Palestinian prisoners?

Yes. I used to direct a television programme called A Date with Freedom. Then I became the one looking for freedom. My work had trained me to read light, listen closely and notice what was in the frame. I kept doing that in prison. Each scene stayed in my head like a scene from a horror film. I was the person it was happening to, already trying to anticipate what would come next.

There was light that never went out, or darkness that never lifted. I remember the absence of shadows, the narrow field of vision, the walls all one colour, the iron cages. Then there were the blindfolds, the restraints on our wrists and ankles, the lack of sleep, and the constant hunger. I understood how those things could strip away my sense of where I was and how much time had passed.

I could still pick out the layers of sound. I heard the echo of iron doors, the rattle of restraints, the timing of footsteps. I could hear people screaming under torture nearby and dogs barking. There was the sound of weapons, stun grenades, smoke grenades, and electric shocks. Sometimes we had to keep silent. At other times the noise never stopped. To my ear, there was a deliberate rhythm to it. It governed what I paid attention to and kept my body tense.

There was smell, too. I could smell my own flesh rotting. There was pepper spray in our eyes, and disease spread among us. I felt the purpose was to keep me so occupied with what was happening to my own body that all five of my senses were in their hands.
When Wesam was recording your testimony, did you hesitate to include any of the humiliating abuse? What made you decide to leave those details in the book?

Yes. I had been threatened with death if I spoke about what happened in prison. The threat extended to my family. And there was the humiliation itself. What they had done was meant to strip me of my dignity. To remember it and describe it in detail meant living through it again. With some of the most intimate details, I kept thinking about my children. How would they read those words? How would my family and the people around us read them?

With Wesam, I felt safe enough to speak. He recorded what I said carefully, without exaggerating or turning it into something meant to shock people. I trusted him with those details because I wanted an honest account to survive for the people who come after us.

In the third scene, you describe death at Sde Teiman as “a wish deferred, a simple dream denied you as long as you kept breathing”. If you feel able to speak about it, what kept that wish from becoming a reality?

I think there was still a witness inside me. Even when death seemed like a dream, some part of me could still find the words to describe what was happening. That part of me had not given up. I still had a story to tell.

In describing the “disco” torture, you say you learned that bodies could be tested like instruments. What do you think the purpose was? Was it to obtain information, or to make a person feel reduced to a body until they stopped resisting?

On the surface, they wanted information. At a deeper level, I felt they were trying to break the connection between me and my own body. They could treat it as an instrument, test it, and see how it responded. To me, that was part of the purpose of the torture.
The book describes the Sde Teiman military base as “the Auschwitz of Palestine”. What does it mean to you to have your experience placed in that historical frame?

For me, the comparison asks something of the reader. The name Auschwitz still makes people ask, “How did the world allow this to happen?” Auschwitz has its own history as part of a system built to exterminate an entire people on an industrial scale. I understand the author’s comparison as an appeal to the reader’s conscience. I want someone reading about Sde Teiman to pause before turning the page as they might after any other news story, and to consider where they stand on what happened there.
What I lived through was beyond what I could put into ordinary words. That is what the comparison means to me. It reaches for some of the hardest words history has given us.
The book recounts prolonged solitary confinement and systematic attempts at humiliation. When you were alone, was there anything that helped you keep track of time or hold on to your sense of self?

My clock was the day’s only meal. When they gave me half a slice of mouldy bread, I knew the day was ending. There was another way to mark time. Four times a day came what we called “the count”, part of the daily routine of torture.

In isolation, I began to lose my sense of time and of myself together. I felt suspended between life and death, trying to stay alive. One thing I could still do was think about how I would bear witness later. The question in my mind gradually changed from “Why is this happening to me?” to “How will I tell this afterwards?”

The book bears witness to “the steadfastness of a people whose political existence cannot be extinguished”. Where do you see that steadfastness in Gaza after Israel’s genocidal war? In rebuilding, in continuing to tell stories, or in something quieter?

You can rebuild a house and someone can tear it down again. You can tell a story and people can forget it. What makes both acts possible is something quieter. In Gaza, we go on living without asking permission. We refuse to become a memory. To me, steadfastness is holding on to your full humanity in a place where you were meant to be nothing.
A closing word?

If you want to know who I am, I am one of those who came back from hell. And if you want to know something about the place I call Israel’s Guantánamo, I can tell you this. There, those who died were the ones who escaped, and those who survived were the ones who died. We lived between this world and the next, through the terrors of the hereafter. Our flesh began to decay while we were still alive. But they will never succeed in killing off the witnesses. This is our land.
Wesam Afifa

Osama is a television director, and you have divided the book into 36 “scenes”, which you call “journeys into the circles of hell”. Was the scene-based structure a way of letting Osama tell his story in the language he is most familiar with?

Yes. The structure grew out of both Osama’s way of telling his story and the visual language we shared through our work in television. I first met him when I was overseeing a local Palestinian television channel. He joined our team as a junior director about two years before the war.

When we met after his release, he began describing the horrors he had endured in Israeli detention, including at Sde Teiman. As I listened, I felt he was trying to convey something beyond an account of violations. He was reconstructing scenes, helping me picture what he had lived through and understand the human experience within the suffering.

The television director I had known was now a survivor whose own life had become a succession of horrifying scenes. His background as a director and mine in journalism and television helped shape the book’s 36 scenes, each revealing part of a larger, devastating picture.

The structure also leaves open the possibility of a future documentary or dramatic adaptation. Osama wanted his experience to reach people through every available medium and expressed a willingness to participate in a television or film production.

The Palestinian Center for Prisoners’ Advocacy has praised the book as a “historical record documenting an exceptional period in the history of Israeli prisons”. Beyond preserving memory, what role does such firsthand testimony play in the broader documentation of the Palestinian experience?

Documenting an exceptional period in the history of Israeli prisons was one of the book’s central purposes. Palestinian prison literature has long preserved the experiences of successive generations. But I believe the scale and forms of abuse inflicted on Palestinian prisoners after October 7 make this a period that demands particular attention and documentation.

These experiences must become part of Palestinian collective memory and the world’s memory. If the world accepts what happened in places such as Sde Teiman, the consequences extend beyond Palestine. Silence allows such practices to become acceptable and creates the conditions for their repetition elsewhere.

Firsthand testimony also carries a demand for accountability. By preserving Osama’s account, we place it before the international community, human rights organisations and those pursuing justice for victims. The testimony remains available to be examined alongside other evidence, even when accountability is delayed. It tells those responsible that the passage of time will not erase what happened.

The book also connects imprisonment to the wider Palestinian experience during the genocidal war on Gaza. Osama witnessed and covered horrific events as a cameraman and television director in the war’s first weeks, before becoming a prisoner himself. His account takes the reader through both experiences, bringing together what he witnessed outside detention and what he endured inside it.
Through one person’s story, readers can begin to grasp the human meaning of events that might otherwise reach them only as figures or headlines.
Did Osama have doubts about publishing the book, whether from fear of retaliation or concern that telling his story might revive his trauma? What did you say to him at those moments?

Yes. Osama initially had doubts and felt anxious and afraid. Simply speaking about what he had endured was painful. As I listened and recorded his testimony, he shared horrifying details that he told me he had never discussed even with his wife or family.

At times, I encouraged him because I felt the world needed to hear the truth. He knew these conversations would become a book, and possibly lead to other ways of telling his story. That purpose seemed to give him courage: as both a journalist and a survivor, he could help expose what had happened.

But the suffering did not end with his release. We stopped repeatedly when the memories became too difficult. These included accounts of rape using dogs, deaths and torture he had witnessed, and torture he described as so severe that he lost his memory for several days.

Sometimes he fell silent. I sensed that he was trying not to let me see how close he was to breaking down. Speaking took considerable courage, and I do not want to make that process sound easier than it was.

Our existing friendship and professional relationship helped. He was speaking to someone he knew and trusted, and I believe that made it easier to share experiences he might have struggled to recount to an unfamiliar writer.
The introduction says this is “a book that should never have been written”. What do you hope readers will take away from Osama’s account of suffering, resilience, and resistance?

When I wrote that this was “a book that should never have been written”, I was thinking about how painful it would be even to read these experiences. There were moments when I asked myself: what would make someone living in comfort choose to enter this world of suffering? How could I ask a reader to follow another human being into pain so relentless that death itself begins to seem like a relief?

Yet I wanted readers to understand that the world extends beyond what they see from the safety of their own lives. Others inhabit a profound darkness, subjected to occupation and to deliberate, sadistic cruelty. I also wanted them to encounter the human capacity to endure within that darkness: the struggle to stay alive and find a way out.

For me, survival remains incomplete when a survivor’s experience goes unheard. Someone who has endured torture can remain captive to its pain long after leaving prison, especially when the world ignores what happened and their story stays buried behind the walls they have physically escaped.

I hope readers will listen, feel solidarity and anger, and allow those feelings to move them to act. Knowing that others have read, understood, and responded may ease some of the survivor’s sense of isolation. The book cannot undo what Osama endured. But it can help carry his testimony into the world, where others can acknowledge it and take responsibility for how they respond.
You are a journalist from Gaza with over 30 years of experience. How did you handle grief or anger while documenting Osama’s prison experience?

Listening to Osama brought deep sadness and anger, partly because his experience touched memories of my own imprisonment. I was 17 when Israeli forces arrested me during the First Intifada. I spent a year in detention and underwent interrogation. What I endured was only a fraction of what Osama described, but I recognised something of the helplessness, the waiting, and the hope of release. That shared experience helped me understand some of what lay beneath his words.

My years in journalism also shaped how I listened. I have covered successive uprisings and wars and documented grave violations. I have lost friends and relatives, and known many people who experienced imprisonment. That background helped me speak with Osama and give him the space to recount his experience.

I was also living through this war myself. During it, I met other released prisoners and heard accounts of suffering that, to my understanding, marked an exceptional period even within the long history of Palestinian imprisonment. Those testimonies gave me a broader context for understanding Osama’s account.

I cannot say that professional experience insulated me from grief or anger. It helped me give those feelings a purpose through the work: listening carefully, documenting his experience, and finding language that could bring readers closer to it. The challenge was to convey the depth of his suffering while allowing readers to see and understand the person who had endured it.
Did you consider the book’s potential use as evidence in a legal or advocacy context? If so, did that influence how you approached the details?

The legal dimension was always present because we were documenting an experience of imprisonment and abuse. Osama had already given statements to several local and international human rights organisations. I wanted the book to convey dimensions of his experience that I felt those statements could not fully capture.

Such statements record acts, conditions and procedures, but I felt there was more to communicate about the pain, humiliation and inner life of the person subjected to them. A statement might record that he had been subjected to attempted rape using dogs. In the book, we sought to convey the scene as Osama described experiencing it: the dogs’ panting and howling, his fear, and the physical and emotional suffering. Those details bring the reader closer to the lived experience behind the testimony.
I wanted readers to ask themselves: what if I were in Osama’s place? What would it mean to endure this?

That intention shaped the attention I gave to the details in his testimony. I saw the book as a work of prison literature, a record that could be examined in a legal context, and a possible foundation for a future film or television production. Across those possibilities, my central concern was to communicate his experience in its human depth.
